questions.q: GaAs is made of gallium (group III) and arsenic (group V). Why does it form a semiconductor crystal much like silicon (group IV)?
options: On average each atom has four bonding electrons, as in silicon
Gallium and arsenic both have exactly four outer electrons, as silicon does
Arsenic gives all its electrons to gallium, so the crystal has none to spare
Each arsenic atom gives one free electron, so GaAs conducts like n-type silicon
questions.explain: Gallium has three outer electrons and arsenic five, so on average each atom has four, like silicon, and they form the same kind of tetrahedral bonds. GaAs, InP and GaN are the best-known III–V compounds.

questions.q: The map shows band gap against lattice constant (atom spacing). Why can AlGaAs be grown on GaAs at any composition?
questions.alt: Band gap against lattice constant for common cubic semiconductors, with alloy lines joining pairs of compounds
options: AlAs and GaAs have almost the same atom spacing, so every mix of them fits GaAs
AlAs and GaAs have the same band gap, so every mix of them has that gap too
Aluminium atoms are so small that they fit anywhere in the GaAs crystal
AlGaAs has a larger band gap, so it always grows well on a smaller-gap crystal
questions.explain: Layers grow cleanly on each other only if their atom spacings match. AlAs and GaAs differ by only 0.14%, so AlGaAs matches GaAs at any composition, while its gap can still be chosen.

questions.q: Why does GaAs give out light efficiently while silicon does not?
options: In GaAs the electron drops straight to a hole; in silicon it must also change momentum
GaAs has a much larger band gap than silicon, so its electrons fall further and give brighter light
Silicon absorbs all the light it gives out, so none can escape from the crystal
Silicon's electrons are too heavy to give out photons
questions.explain: A photon carries almost no momentum. In GaAs (a direct gap) the electron drops straight down and emits light. In silicon (an indirect gap) it must also change momentum, which needs a phonon, so the light is weak.

questions.q: The graphs show electron velocity against electric field for five materials, on a linear scale (left) and a log scale (right). Which materials are fastest at very high fields?
questions.alt: Electron drift velocity against electric field for Si, GaAs, InGaAs, 4H-SiC and GaN, with a linear field axis (left) and a log field axis (right)
options: The wide-gap materials, GaN and SiC
GaAs and InGaAs, which keep their peak velocity
Silicon, whose velocity keeps rising with field
All five are equally fast at very high fields
questions.explain: GaAs and InGaAs are fastest at low fields but fall back after their peak. The wide-gap GaN and SiC saturate later but at a higher speed, which matters for high-power, high-frequency devices.

questions.q: Why does a HEMT (high-electron-mobility transistor) put its donor atoms in a separate layer above the channel?
options: Their electrons then travel in clean GaAs, away from the ions that scatter them
In a separate layer they make the channel p-type, which is faster
In the channel they would trap the electrons, so none could move
The donors need to be close to the gate so that the gate can switch them
questions.explain: Donors supply electrons but also scatter them. Put the donors in a layer above the channel: their electrons fall into clean GaAs and travel without hitting the ions, an express lane.

questions.q: True or false: in a GaN HEMT, as in a GaAs HEMT, the channel electrons must come from a doped donor layer.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. AlGaN and GaN crystals are electrically polarised. The change in polarisation at the interface pulls in about ten times more electrons than an AlGaAs/GaAs HEMT holds, with no doping at all.

questions.q: In a heterojunction bipolar transistor (HBT), what does the wider-gap emitter do?
options: It blocks holes leaking back from the base, so the base can be heavily doped
It lowers the emitter's resistance, so more electrons are injected
It blocks electrons from entering the base, cutting the leakage current
It makes the transistor switch on at zero voltage, so it needs no supply
questions.explain: Holes leaking back into the emitter waste current. A wider-gap emitter adds a wall in the valence band that stops them but not the electrons, so the base can be heavily doped: lower resistance and higher speed.

questions.q: The picture shows, to scale, the layers in silicon and GaN that block 600 V. Why can the GaN layer be so much thinner?
questions.alt: Two blocking layers for 600 V drawn to scale: silicon 40 µm thick and lightly doped; GaN 3.6 µm thick and doped 100 times more
options: GaN can withstand about ten times silicon's electric field before breaking down
GaN electrons are so fast that they cross the layer before breakdown starts
GaN is a better conductor of heat, so it needs less material
GaN is an insulator, so any thickness of it blocks the voltage
questions.explain: SiC and GaN withstand about ten times silicon's critical field. The blocking layer can be ten times thinner and a hundred times more heavily doped, so its resistance is hundreds of times lower.

questions.q: The picture compares how 8 electrons fill the states in a silicon channel and in an InGaAs channel. Why does InGaAs give less charge per volt of gate voltage, despite its faster electrons?
questions.alt: 8 electrons filling the energy levels in a silicon channel (left) and in an InGaAs channel (right)
options: Light electrons have few states per energy, so they must fill higher ones, which costs gate voltage
Its electrons are heavier than silicon's, so the gate cannot move them as easily
Its gate oxide is much thicker than silicon's, so the gate is further from the channel
Its electrons leak out of the channel into the substrate before they reach the drain
questions.explain: A light mass means few states at each energy. To hold the same charge, InGaAs electrons must fill states much higher up, and that is paid for with gate voltage: faster electrons, but fewer of them (the density-of-states bottleneck).

questions.q: Apart from charge per volt, what else has kept III–V compounds out of CMOS processors?
options: Their holes are no faster than silicon's, and they have no clean native oxide for the gate
They cannot be made into transistors smaller than 1 µm
They conduct electricity so poorly that the chips would need very high voltages
Their band gaps are too large to switch at 1 V
questions.explain: CMOS needs fast p-channels too, and III–V holes are no better than silicon's; GaAs has no clean native oxide, and deposited ones trap charge. Instead, III–Vs join silicon for what it cannot do: GaN power and RF, and lasers on silicon photonics.
